passages.t: The poor man deserted, and a prudent wife from the LORD
passages.happening:
‘Better a poor man who walks with integrity than a fool whose lips are perverse’ (verse 1). ‘Even zeal is no good without knowledge’ (verse 2). ‘A man’s own folly subverts his way, yet his heart rages against the LORD’ (verse 3).

‘Wealth attracts many friends, but a poor man is deserted by his friend’ (verse 4). ‘Many seek the favor of the prince, and everyone is a friend of the gift giver’ (verse 6). Even a poor man's own brothers turn against him, and his friends keep away; he pleads with them, and they are nowhere to be found (verse 7). Twice the chapter says that ‘A false witness will not go unpunished’ (verses 5 and 9).

‘A man’s insight gives him patience, and his virtue is to overlook an offense’ (verse 11). A king's rage is like a lion's roar, and his favor like dew on the grass (verse 12). ‘A foolish son is his father’s ruin, and a quarrelsome wife is like a constant dripping’ (verse 13). ‘Houses and wealth are inherited from fathers, but a prudent wife is from the LORD’ (verse 14).
passages.hearers:
This chapter looks at who is valued and who is abandoned. It does not pretend that wealth wins no friends or that poverty keeps them. But it sets all of that under God's judgment and care, and verse 1 puts a poor man with integrity above a rich fool.

Verse 3 is sharp and honest: people ruin their own lives by folly and then blame God for it.

Verse 7 is unusual in having three lines instead of two. Many scholars think the last line is the remnant of another saying whose other half has been lost.

Israelite houses had flat roofs of beams, branches and packed clay, and in the winter rains they leaked. A drip that never stopped was a familiar misery. Verse 13 is not a comment on women in general, since the very next verse calls a prudent wife a gift from the LORD. It is a frank picture of a home without peace.

Verse 12 sets a lion's roar, the most feared sound in Israel's hills, beside dew on the grass, the gift that kept summer crops alive in the dry months.
passages.later: Job knew the desertion of verses 4 and 7: ‘But my brothers are as faithless as wadis’ (Job 6:15). So did the psalmist: ‘My beloved and friends shun my disease, and my kinsmen stand at a distance’ (Psalm 38:11). And Paul gives the counsel of verse 11: ‘Bear with one another and forgive any complaint you may have against someone else’ (Colossians 3:13).
passages.asks: The poor man's friends disappeared when he had nothing to give. Ask whether your friendships depend on what people can offer you. And ask whether you have blamed God for trouble that your own choices made.

passages.t: A loan to the LORD, and his purpose that stands
passages.happening:
‘Laziness brings on deep sleep, and an idle soul will suffer hunger’ (verse 15). ‘He who keeps a commandment preserves his soul’ (verse 16).

“Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD, and He will repay the lender” (verse 17).

‘Discipline your son, for in that there is hope; do not be party to his death’ (verse 18). ‘A man of great anger must pay the penalty; if you rescue him, you will have to do so again’ (verse 19). ‘Listen to counsel and accept discipline, that you may be wise the rest of your days’ (verse 20).

“Many plans are in a man’s heart, but the purpose of the LORD will prevail” (verse 21). ‘The desire of a man is loving devotion; better to be poor than a liar’ (verse 22). ‘The fear of the LORD leads to life, that one may rest content’ (verse 23).
passages.hearers:
Verse 17 draws on Israel's laws about lending. The law told Israelites to lend freely to a poor brother without charging interest, and every seventh year brought release of debts. Such loans were often never repaid, and a lender could count them as lost. Proverbs sees them differently. Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD himself, and he repays.

Verse 18's second line is difficult. It may warn a parent not to let discipline go so far as to cause a child's death. Or, as many interpreters read it, it may warn a parent not to contribute to a child's ruin by never correcting at all. Neither reading gives anyone a warrant to harm a child.

Abuse of a child is a crime. It is to be reported to the police and the proper authorities, not handled quietly inside a church. If a child is in danger, or you know of a child being harmed, contact the police or your local child protection service now. If you were harmed as a child, what was done to you was wrong, and it was not your fault. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

Verse 21 says again what 16:1 and 16:9 said. People make many plans, and God's purpose stands.
passages.later: The law says, ‘If you lend money to one of My people among you who is poor, you must not act as a creditor to him’ (Exodus 22:25). And the psalm says of God's purpose: ‘The counsel of the LORD stands forever, the purposes of His heart to all generations’ (Psalm 33:11).
passages.hard:
Proverbs often links poverty with laziness (verse 15). Is it saying the poor deserve their poverty?

Proverbs does say that laziness leads to want, and verses 15 and 24 make the point sharply. But the book never offers laziness as the only explanation, and a reader who takes it that way misreads it. In these same chapters poverty also comes from injustice (13:23), from oppression by the powerful (14:31; 22:16, 22), from dishonest dealing, and from plain misfortune. The same chapter that mocks the slacker puts the poor man with integrity above a rich fool (verse 1), and says that kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD (verse 17).

The sayings about laziness are warnings to the young reader about his own conduct. They are not a tool for judging the poor. They tell him that if he sleeps through harvest he will go hungry. They do not tell him that every hungry person slept through harvest. Some are poor through no fault of their own, and the book is equally clear that God defends them.
passages.asks: Kindness to the poor is a loan to the LORD. Ask whom you could help this week without expecting anything back. And ask which of your plans you need to hold more loosely, since his purpose is the one that stands.

passages.t: A hand in the dish, and a son who shames his parents
passages.happening:
‘The slacker buries his hand in the dish; he will not even bring it back to his mouth’ (verse 24).

When a mocker is punished, the simple learn from it, and when the discerning are corrected, they gain knowledge (verse 25). ‘He who assaults his father or evicts his mother is a son who brings shame and disgrace’ (verse 26).

Then the father speaks directly: ‘If you cease to hear instruction, my son, you will stray from the words of knowledge’ (verse 27). ‘A corrupt witness mocks justice’ (verse 28), and judgment waits for mockers (verse 29).
passages.hearers:
Meals were eaten by hand from a shared dish, with bread used to scoop up food. The slacker gets his hand into the dish and is too lazy to lift it back to his mouth. The exaggeration makes laziness absurd, a trick Proverbs uses often.

Verse 26 describes a son who attacks his father or drives out his mother. There were no pensions. Aging parents depended on their children for food, shelter and protection, and the command to honor father and mother carried that practical weight. Driving out a widowed mother could leave her with nothing.

Verse 27 is the first time since the opening chapters that the father speaks to his son directly. These sayings are still teaching passed from one generation to the next.
passages.later: The commandment stands behind verse 26: ‘Honor your father and mother, so that your days may be long in the land’ (Exodus 20:12).
passages.asks: The chapter ends with a son and his aging parents. Ask how you honor your parents now, whatever their age and whatever your story with them. And ask whether you have stopped listening to instruction anywhere in your life.
